# Draft:International Bystander Awareness Day

= International Bystander Awareness Day =
International Bystander Awareness Day is an annual observance held on 13 March that promotes public awareness of bystander intervention and encourages individuals to take safe, responsible action when witnessing harassment, hate crime, violence or other harmful behaviour. The day highlights the role of ordinary people in preventing harm, supporting those at risk and challenging abuse in everyday settings.
The observance originated in the United Kingdom as National Bystander Awareness Day, before expanding internationally.
Background
The principles underlying bystander awareness are rooted in social psychology research on the bystander effect, a term introduced by psychologists John M. Darley and Bibb Latané in the late 1960s. Their research demonstrated that individuals are statistically less likely to intervene in emergencies when others are present, often due to diffusion of responsibility or uncertainty about how to act.
Public discussion of bystander behaviour intensified following the 1964 murder of Catherine “Kitty” Genovese in New York City, which became widely cited in academic and public discourse on collective responsibility and social response to violence. Although later reporting corrected aspects of the original narrative, the case played a significant role in shaping research and awareness around bystander inaction.
History
National Bystander Awareness Day was established in the United Kingdom in 2019 by the community safety and anti-hate organisation [https://communitiesinc.org.uk/ Communities Inc.] The initiative was developed to address concerns around hate crime, harassment and public safety, with an emphasis on empowering members of the public to recognise harmful behaviour and intervene safely.
The day focused on education, awareness-raising and promoting practical approaches to bystander intervention, including recognising risk, de-escalation and reporting. Early observances were marked through community engagement activities, training programmes and public campaigns across the UK.
In 2023, the initiative expanded beyond the UK and was re-launched as International Bystander Awareness Day, reflecting growing international interest in bystander intervention as a preventative approach to hate, harassment and violence.
Observance
International Bystander Awareness Day is observed annually on 13 March. Activities associated with the day typically include:
* Public awareness campaigns on bystander responsibility
* Active bystander training and education
* Community and workplace safety initiatives
* Events focused on hate crime prevention and safeguarding
In the United Kingdom, public bodies and transport authorities have marked the day by supporting free active bystander training for members of the public. For example, Transport for London (TfL) has funded training sessions aimed at addressing harassment and hate incidents on public transport.
Aims
The stated aims of International Bystander Awareness Day include:
* Increasing public understanding of the bystander effect
* Encouraging safe and proportionate intervention
* Reducing barriers to action such as fear or uncertainty
* Promoting reporting and support where direct intervention is not possible
* Supporting community responsibility and cohesion
The observance is commonly associated with wider work on hate crime prevention, violence against women and girls, safeguarding and public safety education.
